title: Suffering Humans Practice Here, The Heart Sutra
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of finding balance between taking life seriously and holding it lightly with humility, suggesting that this paradoxical approach can help us cultivate wisdom, compassion, and liberation from our attachments and ego. By embracing the concept of "emptiness," we can release our assumptions and projections onto the world, leading to a softer boundary between ourselves and others and a greater sense of freedom and openness. This balance allows us to approach life with a sense of hope and prayer for freedom, rather than just intellectual understanding, in order to live with wisdom and kindness.

sentences.text: Good morning.
Someone was telling me the other day, she had first met me in a different context, presenting at a class.
And she said, "Yeah, you seemed so warm and friendly.
And then I had to get to know you again at the Zen center, and you seemed sort of formal and cold."
So I thought I'd try to manage a good, good morning.
Because we have both of these, right?
And don't you think we need both?
Isn't it good to have space to be friendly and cheerful, and also space to just be quiet together?
Why would that only be the domain of being alone?
To get to be quiet and reserved together is also good, I think.
So anyway, I'm so glad to be here.
I'm so glad you're here.
We're experimenting with a new schedule.
Of course, there are a few kinks to work out, and that's all right.
And here we are.
Great.
You probably know we're trying this Sunday 10 a.m. meeting.
It's hard not to call it church time, because that's what it is, I guess.
I never went to church, but is this church time?
More or less?
Nine or 11.
At least we're charting our own way there.
We're going to do this once a month in 2020, the first Sunday of every month.
Before, we thought we would have to skip March, but now it turns out we can do March too, so every month, whatever the first Sunday is.
We'll try this.
We'll play with this.
And what a great start.
And then maybe in '21, if we're all still here, we'll do more than once a month, maybe every week.
So in a way, it's just another meeting.
No big deal.
Doing what we do here, just getting together to sit, breathe, be, chant and bow, discuss the Dharma.
Not a big deal, but also a kind of big deal moment.
Because of our origins as a small sitting group, we started out by sharing a Dharma hall with three other groups.
The only real way to do that was that everybody got a weeknight.
We couldn't have had anybody do every weekend, because then what would all the other groups do if you were there on the weekend?
So not much happened on the weekend.
We'd do a weeknight.
And so we've carried that forward.
Fast forward 25 years and, oh, we can meet on the weekend.
Wow, cool.
We'll still have Wednesday night as a primary practice, I think, too.
But nice, especially in the winter, right, to not drive here at night in the dark, slippery conditions, if that's not safe for you.
So I want to thank everybody for endorsing that idea with your bodies.
That's the only vote that really counts.
We have our opinions.
And I want to thank the practice committee for supporting the idea, albeit with some wise reservations.
"What?
Another thing to do?"
And the board, too.
And I especially thank Chris to my right, Shudo, Chris Burkhart, who are really taking on the coordinating of this monthly project in a helpful way.
They've taken a big load off me.
And also, this all fits together because it's a very appropriate thing for Chris to do, because we gave her a promotion.
This is hot off the presses.
In one of the monastic positions that we had not so far had here, a Zen practice position we've not so far had, is called Tanto.
And the Tanto is the head of practice.

Chris and I talked about this for the better part of a year, and then we talked about it with the practice committee, and I offered her this position of Tanto, head of practice, and she accepted, which I'm grateful for.
And so the Tanto really helps the Sangha by being the teacher on the ground.
She'll sit in the Zen-do in a special seat.
She'll support the Yino, who is sitting right next to her.
And she'll support the Sangha with some of the details of how we do this way of being together, how we do this way of practice.
The only part of her job description we've figured out so far in words beyond that is she'll be the mentor of forms.
The mentor of forms.
We like "mentor" better than some other, more authoritarian words that we thought of.
Because there is a particular way that we move and hold our bodies that we've received through this tradition, and it's a lot to take in, and I hesitate to go around correcting people or anything.
So Chris will, in some organized way, gradually inform us and support us in entering that format of being together a little more deeply.
And what's cool is that there's an internal resonance with that.
This way of being that we've received supports a certain kind of awareness and a certain kind of uprightness and a certain kind of stability.
So in a way, what does it really matter if the tips of your fingers are in line with your nose when you make the gassho movement?
What's wrong with this or this?
But actually there's a particular way to do it, and we all do it the same way, and there's a feeling to that.
Look for useful little tips and tricks and other helpful advice from Chris.
So thanks, Chris.
And I could go on about every single person here and all the great things you're doing, but I also want to thank someone who's not here.
Hannah Sullivan, who has just completed two years as the Eno, the meditation hall coordinator.
So we'll thank her formally in a couple of weeks.
And I want to thank Bob Penny, who's literally been here from the beginning, for stepping into this role now.
He's doing the stuff.
So thanks, Bob.
And I think that's really cool, that this thing's so endless.
No matter how long you're here, there's always more stuff to learn and do and try and stretch yourself.
So it's wonderful that Bob's doing that.
We're all doing that all the time, trying to learn and grow and stretch ourselves.
And there's really a lot of commitment in this room.
I wonder how many cumulative years of meditation practice are in this room.
Hundreds, probably.
And it's not so easy to sit yourself down and watch your shit.
Watch your breath, watch your body, watch your mind.
You could distract yourself and do something else.
That's so helpful, right?
So it's wonderful that we have this room full of people committed to this, whatever you call it.
It expresses in an individual way, but also so universal, this way of being, this way of practice.
And it really does take commitment.
Most of us, it's not something we fall into as a desire thing or as a preference thing.
You get home and you're tired and you think to yourself, what should I do now?
And not often, at least for me, maybe it's true for you, but not often for me do I think, "I know.
Formal meditation practice, that's what I think."
But more and more it occurs to me, "Did I practice today?
It would really help me to practice."
All right.
And I feel so much better.
And I'm so inspired when I come here.
So it takes commitment.
And commitment is interesting.
What are we really committing to?
Our lives are full of all kinds of commitments, some of which we seem to make actively, some which seem to be made for us.
And what's the spirit that we bring to our commitments?
I'm really thinking about that.
You all committed this morning to Zen practice and to the community.
So what is it you're committing to right now?
Who is it you're committing to?
And how does it really feel to show up in your commitment?
What's the energy of it?
What's the feeling in the body?
What's the emotional tone?
Of course, that varies.
That varies.
But nothing's really going to happen unless we're committed to it.
We have to really give it a try.
So that's what we're doing with this Sunday schedule, this Sunday practice.
We're trying to be serious about it.
If this is going to be useful to the community of Red Cedar Zen or the community of Bellingham or the world, we have to be serious.
We have to actually really give it a try.
It can't be too tentative.
And it matters.
But it seems like on the other hand, if we're too tight about it, if we have a closed and rigid spirit, it won't be so great.
It won't be so helpful.
It will kind of backfire, and we'll suffer.
And we'll spread suffering to others even with our well-intentioned commitment.
You know what I mean?
Sometimes a commitment, our attempt to be helpful and to offer something, has this kind of tight quality to it.
And that's toxic.
So I just keep thinking about this a lot in my life.
And what keeps coming to me is that maybe it's best, if I can really do a good job, taking my life more seriously, but also holding it lightly with humility.
Because I don't even really know what my life is.
Do you know what your life is?
I'm thinking that this Zen practice is such a great way to experiment with this: taking our life seriously and holding it lightly.
We've learned so many lessons here over the decades around this.

We're like custodians of a tradition, so we're trying to take this seriously and carry forward Soto Zen as it was taught to us and received through Norman Fischer and Suzuki Roshi and the other teachers and mentors and supporters who've been involved.
And we have a little table now in the lobby of some of those teachers who have passed on.
But sometimes we get a little tight about it.
We suffer and there's conflicts.
Feelings get hurt.
And then we learn from that.
Oops, a little too much this way, a little too much that way.
Thankfully there's fewer hurt feelings the last decade or so.
That's nice for me.
But it still happens and I'm sorry when it happens.
It's not good to have hurt feelings.
And yet I think if we're going to take this practice seriously, in our lives seriously, in each other seriously, there's going to be hurt feelings sometimes.
It's just a question of how we practice with it.
So I think maybe we need to sign over the doorway there that says, "FYI, humans practice here."
Unless anyone has some other ideas.
They all look so peaceful.
How about those ones with the special clothes on?
They must be special.
Or maybe we could have that printed, "FYI, suffering humans practice here."
And then we can handwrite a little carrot.
Or no, "humans practice here."
We can put a little carrot and say, "suffering humans practice here."
Because that's why we're here really.
We're all pretty competent and well regulated and well spoken and so on and so forth, right?
But we're all suffering too.
So take it seriously and hold it lightly.
Which I think is more or less what the Heart Sutra, we were just chanting, is trying to tell us.
Take it seriously, but hold it lightly.
Why?
Well, not just because that might be smart or skillful or work out the best in the end, which probably is true.
But the Heart Sutra takes it a big step further.
It's really saying, why?
Because actually there's nothing whatsoever to hold on to tightly anyway.
So what are you so uptight about, holding on to nothing?
Holding on to emptiness.
It's a strange kind of dense text with all of its negation and technical language.
But I think that's kind of what it's trying to remind us.
Take this life, suffering, and this possibility of freedom from suffering, this possibility of wisdom and compassion, this possibility of saving all beings.
Take this seriously, but you need to understand what it is.
It's something that can only be held lightly because of its true nature.
Suzuki Roshi had an interesting way of talking about this.
Are you hearing me okay?
I got some feedback.
I don't speak up enough.
Are you hearing okay?
Can you wave if you can't hear?
Sometimes I get a little tired.
Let me know if you can't hear.
So here's Suzuki Roshi.
*In the Prajnaparamita Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the most important point, of course, is the idea of emptiness.
Before we understand the idea of emptiness, everything seems to exist substantially.
But we understand, sorry, before we understand the idea of emptiness, everything seems to exist substantially.
But after we realize the emptiness of things, everything becomes real and not substantial.*
*When we realize that everything we see is a part of emptiness, we can have no attachment to any existence.
We realize that everything is just a tentative form and color.
Thus we realize the true meaning of each tentative existence.
When we first hear that everything is a tentative existence, most of us are disappointed.
But this disappointment comes from the wrong view of humans and nature.
It is because our way of observing things is deeply rooted in our self-centered ideas that we are disappointed when we find out that everything has a tentative existence.
But when we actually realize the truth, we will have no suffering.*
That's great about these teachings.
They say some confusing philosophical thing.
At the end they say, if you understand this, you will have no suffering.
Now you're like, whoa, wait a minute, read that again.
What was that?
How do I get the no suffering part?
Of course that's the problem.
How do I get the no suffering part?
It doesn't work that way.
So this is an interesting way of talking.
Everything is real.
These teachings are not that it's all just a fantasy.
They're real, but they're not so substantial.
That's what he's saying.
So, a little bit about the text itself.
Depending on your learning style, it might be useful to be looking at the text in the book.
I forget what page it's on, 10 maybe.
Especially the opening section.
Or you can just listen, whatever you prefer.
I just want to unpack a little bit the format of the text because it's very dense.
It starts out with a name: Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.
So this whole little text is actually a short talk, a short little dharma talk, dharma discourse, being given by someone named Avalokiteshvara, who is a bodhisattva, a great awakening being.
Desiree in our service mentioned the great bodhisattva of wisdom, the wisdom beyond wisdom bodhisattva, Avalokiteshvara, or sorry, compassion, saying various things backwards.
I'm trying to take this seriously, try to pay attention.
Anyway, this is the bodhisattva of compassion.
Usually personified as a female figure, which is nice in a very male tradition, I'm sorry to acknowledge.
She's introduced right away, but she doesn't start talking right away.
First it talks about her practice.
It says that she is practicing, deeply practicing prajnaparamita.
And then she saw something.
And then our chant book lacks the quotation marks and also the paragraphs, so it's a little hard to see where it goes from there.
But then there's another name, Shariputra.
So this is a monk whom she's talking to.
So this bodhisattva, great bodhisattva of compassion, has a deep practice experience, and she has a realization and she's talking to this monk, Shariputra, to explain something.
So that's the frame story.
And there's more frame story than that, actually.
This is the short version.
There's a longer version where we find out also that the Buddha is here.
The Buddha is always here.
He's sitting in the background.
He's also doing deep practice, but he's doing a wordless deep practice.
He doesn't want to say anything, or it doesn't occur to him to say anything because of his deep meditation.
But the way it's understood is he empowers Avalokita to say something.
And she says something in response to a question from this monk, so that part's missing.
But we know it's there.
The monk asks the question, "How should a noble son or noble daughter who wishes to engage in the practice of profound perfection of wisdom train?"
So this is an answer to that question, this whole text.
How should a noble son or noble daughter who wishes to engage in the practice of profound perfection of wisdom train?
And another thing that's difficult about our text here is it leaves a few words untranslated.
And one of the phrases in the very beginning it leaves untranslated is this phrase, prajnya paramita, which means perfection of wisdom.
So this answer is so powerful and so famous that for now, just about 2,000 years, it's been chanted every day in practice places everywhere.
Zen practice places, Tibetan practice places, other practice places in this kind of broad umbrella of the Mahayana school.
And we can think about it for sure as a set of directions, a set of instructions.
The question was, how do you do it?
And so here's the answer.

Especially because this text says that if we really do this, if we practice prajna paramita, if we practice this wisdom beyond wisdom that shows us really how things are, helps us understand this strange distinction Suzuki Roshi made between substantiality and reality, substantial and real, it will relieve our suffering.
And it particularly calls out about the middle there that will also free us from our fear.
And the means of this transformation is a study of this thing called emptiness, which is very tricky sounding, emptiness.
Because to be empty is like a bad thing in English.
Empty sounds like a lack.
An empty gas tank is not a good thing, right, for your car.
You're not going to get far.
Sounds hollow.
Sounds like something's missing and it sounds really not too appealing.
But the key thing here is that the emptiness is not pointing to the lack.
The emptiness is pointing to freedom from something.
Things are empty of something that really messes us up.
And that's wonderful.
So it's not gas exactly.
I don't know what it is.
Maybe you filled your gas tank with concrete and now your car's really not going to work, so you better empty the tank now.
I don't know.
And it's really hard to talk about because it sounds very philosophical and abstract, but I think it's very real and very everyday and so common that we don't even see that we do it.
It's baked into our language and our thinking and it really narrows us down and it makes us take things seriously in a way that doesn't benefit us because we're taking the wrong thing seriously.
What I was trying to say is things are empty of a certain kind of rigid, solid... the best word I'd be able to come up with is "inherently," which also sounds very strange.
But if you think about it, we tend to assume that everything has some sort of inherent something in it.
We do it automatically, so quickly.
We say X, Y, or Z makes me happy.
And I think what we're assuming is whatever the thing is, X, Y, or Z, and it's going to be different for each of us, it has some inherent happy-making qualities that we like.
So we want more of those things.
Whereas A, B, and C makes me unhappy and we want less of those things.

And our life becomes a project of adding more of this and taking away more of that according to our assumptions about these inherent qualities in things, in people, in activities, in sensations, in everything, in everything.
I think everything kind of has this built-in something.
And it's like, of course, duh, right?
That's how it is.
And so I think the challenge for us in practicing this is actually to notice that we do this.
So this is the practice of emptiness: to notice the fullness that we put into things.
The maps and projections and assumptions and presumptions that we make all the time.
And that's part of why I started out about us getting mad at each other around the forms and stuff, because we do that to each other, right?
And so we're great teachers for each other in this.
Because we project all kinds of things onto each other.
And it has this quality in it, I think, of sort of an inherent quality.
She's a really nice person.
He's really grouchy, whatever.
And then the way interpersonal life seems to work, we do what we can to make sure that stays true, whatever it is.
Because we want to be right.
We always want to be right.
So we assume a certain sort of inherent quality to things, and then we do what we can to make sure that we're right.
And it all gets kind of stuck, right?
We get stuck, they get stuck, life gets stuck, the world gets stuck, and the world is pretty stuck because of this, isn't it?
So the practice and study and living into and breathing with emptiness is, can I release that?
Can I release that powerful habit, that powerful projection, that powerful assumption that things are inherently this way or that way?
Can I allow everything to empty out into its true reality?
Can I think what Suzuki Roshi is saying?
And then, what's really super duper, is that when we can do that, when we recognize that's how it already is anyway, then the boundaries get softer.
Some teachers decided that emptiness, it does have this really confusing quality, so we really shouldn't use that word, even though it is actually a pretty correct translation of the original term.
So they may use another word like boundless or interdependent or interconnected, which is also the same truth.
Pointing to the same thing.
That when things are empty of separateness, they're full of everythingness.

So emptiness is open and rich and vibrant and surprising and wondrous, which are not the first synonyms we think of when we heard the English word emptiness, so that's why I'm wanting to mention this.
And part of our project here on the Sunday mornings, too, is to try to make a little more sense of the stuff we're chanting.
You ever wonder what all this stuff means?
So we can definitely look at the text as instructions.
And the instructions are strangely written.
And Thich Nhat Hanh, actually, the wonderful Vietnamese Zen teacher, he apparently has been frustrated by the way instructions are written for some 50 or 60 years or something.
So just a few years ago he released a revised version where he improved the instructions in the Heart Sutra, which only a very senior teacher would be audacious enough to do, but he did.
And he has a wonderful book about that that we studied last year.
You can get his book and study it.
The main thing he added is this.
In our text, the different qualities of being are listed off and negated one after the next.
You probably noticed that part: know this, know that, know that, and even not know this, and know that, up to and including know that.
He adds some phrases to these negations to make them make more sense.
The main phrase he adds is "these things are not separate self-entities," which, of course, is trading one awkward phrase for another, but what can you do?
Language itself divides things, right?
These things are not separate self-entities.
So where we have no eyes, no ears, no nose, and so on, he has "the six sense organs are also not separate self-entities."

The reason we're talking about eyes and ears and noses isn't that this is supposed to be an anatomy lesson, but to recognize deeply that the way we construct our world is through the senses and the mind.
The eyes are not a neutral party, even though we sometimes think that too, which goes with the idea of everything being inherently one way, right?
We say, "I saw it with my own eyes."
That is irrefutable truth of reality, right?
"I saw it with my own eyes."
This is English, you know?
But actually there's more of a dance going on, as we all know.
The eyes see something, there's some interaction with consciousness, some interaction with our memories, and then we construct what we see.
That's really what's happening if we pay attention, but we forget that because we're busy, we're going along.
The sad thing is we're busily going along creating a world full of suffering and separation, so that's why these teachings are so treasured.
What if we took a fresh look at everything?
Everything we see, hear, smell, think, touch, taste, assume.
That would be a good thing.
Probably Thich Nhat Hanh's improvement to the Heart Sutra as instructions is really useful.
I didn't really chant that great, but it's a good improvement to the instructions.
But maybe it's also good not to think of this as instructions, but to think of it more, or also, as a prayer, as an expression of hope, as a deep wish for all of us and for the world.
So maybe if I manage to keep teaching until my late eighties and write a hundred books like Thich Nhat Hanh, I'll release my version.
And maybe it'll be something more like: May we someday be free from our limited views and see that all dharmas are imbued with emptiness and free.
May we someday be free from our narrow-mindedness and our fear and see that what arrives through our eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind is not inherently one way or another and is free.
May we someday be free from trying to lock down everything into understandable concepts with me in the middle.
May we someday be free.
May we someday be free for all beings.
I've got to work on the poetry of it.
So maybe we can also hear the Heart Sutra that way, is what I'm trying to say: as a prayer, as a hope.
And hopes and prayers don't have to make sense.
It's a good thing, you know?
It really would cheapen hopes and prayers if they only had to make sense.
And we're bound up in the whole problem in the first place, right?
The way our sense-making can limit us and divide us and bind us.
When people comment on the Heart Sutra, they tend to focus on the first half, which is instructions, and not so much on the second half, which actually is already a prayer.
So as we chant this going forward, we might notice the prayer qualities of the Heart Sutra that are already there.
That when a bodhisattva relies on prajnaparamita, the mind is [unclear: "about hindrance"].
The mind is [unclear: "about fear"].
And we should know that this prayer, this mantra, is miraculous, is bright, is supreme, is incomparable.
And we should actually pray it.
It says in the end what the prayer is:
*Gathay gathay, para gathay, parasam gathay, bodhisvaha.*
You're supposed to exhale at the end of the svaha.
Svaha.
Mantra, I'm told, means mind protector.
So the mantra of the prajnaparamita is to protect us from a limited mind.
And it's all beyond what we can talk about in words.
So there's nothing wrong with thinking about this stuff and trying to figure it out, and figure out how to do it and what the instructions are, but I think that's not going to be enough.
I think we'll just get frustrated.
We might get a little tight in our seriousness if we're like, "I can't figure this out."
But we also need it as mantra and protection.
These teachings are to protect us from danger.
We tend to think of the danger as being out there somewhere, and that's true, there's danger out there for sure.
But the tradition points out that the main source of danger is our own misunderstood mind.
And actually all the danger out there is from other misunderstood minds.
So this stuff is not just so that we'll feel better, but so that we will be safe and free and able to live in the world that we really need to live in.
That's my little bit of comments for now on the Heart Sutra.

Deep instructions, powerful, deep esoteric teaching, not to keep locking everything down and setting it in concrete, but also as a prayer, as a hope, that we can just lighten up, that we can lighten up in a serious, helpful way, imbued with wisdom and compassion.
And that's the last point.
There's a reason why the Buddha had the Bodhisattva of compassion tell us this.
She offers it to us out of love, and that's how we can offer it to ourselves and to each other.
Thanks for listening to my remarks.
Now we'll continue our experiment by having a little tea and discussion period.
This is all experimenting, but I think what we'll try is to all get up when I'm done talking and rearrange everything into a big circle, with all of us kind of as equal spokes of the wheel.
During that transition, if your body needs a bathroom or something, please take care of yourself.
You can sit in here a while.
Once we're all settled, we'll serve each other tea, whether it's passing the teapots and cups around, serve each other tea.
And once we all have tea, I'll see if I can facilitate something useful by way of discussion and unpacking of all this that makes sense to you.
Okay?
So let's stand up, rearrange.
It's kind of like a little sort of fluid, quiet break, too.
If you need something, bathroom, whatever, we can do that.
Thank you.

Like isn't it good to have space to be friendly and cheerful and also space to just be quiet together, you know? Why would that only be the domain of being alone, you know? To get to be quiet and reserved together is also good, I think. So anyway, I'm so glad to be here. I'm so glad you're here. We're experimenting with a new schedule. Of course, there's a few kinks to work out, and that's all right. And here we are. Great.

So you probably know we're trying this Sunday 10 a.m. meeting. It's hard not to call it church time, because that's what it is, I guess. I never went to church, but is this church time? We'll still have Wednesday night as a primary practice, I think, too. But nice, especially in the winter, right, to not drive here at night in the dark, slippery conditions, if that's not safe for you.

So I want to thank everybody for endorsing that idea with your bodies. That's the only vote that really counts. We have our opinions. And I want to thank the practice committee for supporting the idea, albeit with some wise reservations. What? Another thing to do. And the board, too. And I especially thank Chris to my right, Shudo, Chris Burkhart, who are really taking on the coordinating of this monthly project in a helpful way. They've taken a big load off me. And also, this is all kind of fit together because it's a very appropriate thing for Chris to do because we gave her a promotion. This is hot off the presses.
